name: Omar Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and we keep your answers confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at work is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and supervise eleven people in the returns and service unit of a large appliance company. Before the phones open I check the overnight queue, move staff between complaints and warranty claims, then explain the ugly cases to the regional director. I have an MBA, but the best part is showing a new worker how to calm a caller without making a promise we cannot keep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What weighs on you outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The title sounds better than the pay. I live with my partner, who works shifts at a bakery, and we have less than one month’s bills saved after rent and my MBA loan. There are few similar management posts nearby, so I don’t walk away from a rough month just to make a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is a small change to our queue, not a new set of bosses. I already use a drafting tool now and then for a plain reply, then rewrite it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little tool could speed up routine warranty messages, which is useful. But our rent and loan are tight before any AI, and my partner’s bakery hours change each week. I would still worry about one bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the rest of 2026 I’ll keep our call review and try the approved drafting tool on five routine replies a week, checking every line. If it becomes part of the job next year, I’ll measure whether it frees time for the hard claims; I’ll set aside twenty from each payday if the bakery hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about our household budget, not the small tool. A faster reply does not fill an empty savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count repeat calls on the five messages, not how quickly we sent them. A quick answer that sends a customer back to the phone costs us twice. My director already sees the queue time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if bakery hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty goes back into groceries and bus fare. My partner and I would review the bills together on Sunday, then I would ask for an extra weekend shift at work if there is one. I cannot promise savings from money we have not earned.

say: **AI Plateau** would change only a few routine replies in our queue.
I’d tell the team I still **check** each drafted answer.
think: The tool may help, but **rent and loan payments** already stretch us.
My partner’s changing **bakery hours** can erase a modest saving plan.
do: **Test** five approved draft replies weekly and count repeat customer calls.
**Save** twenty each payday if bakery hours permit.
feel: **Uneasy** about the household budget despite limited AI change.
S0.quote: A quick answer that sends a customer back to the phone costs us twice.
fieldNote: He already uses a **drafting tool** occasionally, but measures customer outcomes rather than speed alone.
The **conditional saving** depends on his partner’s variable bakery hours, not a promised surplus.

steps.text: Test five drafted warranty replies weekly and count repeat calls
Set aside twenty from each payday when bakery hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take first drafts, checks, booking and simple answers out of our unit. We should use the time saved on disputes that need a real conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the director could decide eleven people is too many once the queue drops. I’m a strong manager, but my reports and schedules are screen work too. I think our hours or headcount could shrink, including mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d volunteer for the company’s pilot, then compare repeat complaints and refunds with the old process. I’d ask the director to train our staff on appeal cases before any cuts, and I’d take that paid training if approved. When the new tools spread, I’d apply for an appeals lead opening if one is posted and cut our meal deliveries to protect rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. I can learn the system and show results, but I cannot decide how many people the company keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why volunteer when cuts might follow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone will define the pilot, and I want a worker who handles calls to write the checks. I am not handing the director a blank claim of savings. If the tool worsens refunds, I want that in the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense goes first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We order dinner twice most weeks when both shifts run late. We can cook rice and beans on those nights and put the difference toward the rent buffer. I would tell my partner the reason before changing it.

say: **Drafts and bookings** may leave the unit, freeing time for harder disputes.
I’d want frontline staff to **set pilot checks** before the director judges savings.
think: An eleven-person unit could face **cuts** when the queue shrinks.
My own **reports and schedules** are exposed screen work.
do: **Volunteer** for the company pilot and compare repeat complaints and refunds.
**Request** paid appeals training and take it if approved before staff cuts.
**Replace** two delivered dinners weekly with meals cooked at home.
feel: **Anxious** because he cannot decide the unit’s future size.
S1.quote: I am not handing the director a blank claim of savings.
fieldNote: He welcomes a **measured pilot**, yet expects fewer hours or posts if management values queue speed alone.
His **rent buffer** comes from replacing delivered meals; he would explain the reason to his partner before changing spending.

steps.text: Run the service pilot and compare repeat complaints with the old process
Take paid appeal case training if the director approves it
Replace two weekly delivered dinners with home cooking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell staff AGI by 2028 is a management decision we need numbers for immediately. I would not promise every job survives when cheap AI can handle nearly every thinking task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our replies, warranty checks, rota and reports could all go by 2028. Robots arriving about 2031 matter more to the repair crews than to my desk. With less than a month saved and my partner on variable hours, I expect a deep cut and possibly no job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask the director for a written timetable and a meeting with the worker council, and I’d ask my lender what a payment pause would cost. In 2026 I’d also call two repair firms about supervisor work, though there are few posts here. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I’m cut, I’d take paid service work outside town before waiting for a perfect title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. A spreadsheet cannot pay our rent, and two years is barely enough to build a cushion from this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the worker council ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dates, severance, paid time to learn another role and a named person for each decision. I know my director has costs too. Staff need more than an encouraging speech at a Friday meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner move for that outside job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would have to find a bakery post too, so we would try a commute first. I would not sign a lease in another town on one short contract. We would decide together after the first pay slip.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs a written management timetable and worker input now.
I would not promise staff their **jobs** are safe.
think: Most of my desk work could go in **2028**, before robots reach repair crews around 2031.
Thin savings and variable bakery hours make **job loss** a household crisis.
do: **Request** a meeting with the worker council and director about dates and severance tomorrow.
**Ask** the MBA lender about the cost of a payment pause.
**Call** two repair firms about supervisor posts in 2026.
feel: **Alarmed** about a deep cut before he can build savings.
S2.quote: Staff need more than an encouraging speech at a Friday meeting.
fieldNote: His **public honesty** about job risk matches his private expectation of a cut, unlike a reassuring manager’s script.
The planned **commute** depends on an offer and his partner’s work; he will not sign a second lease on speculation.

steps.text: Request a meeting with the worker council and director about cuts
Call two repair firms about supervisor vacancies this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test where customers still need help. I’d press the director to move staff into appeals and repair coordination while those jobs exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me repay the loan and learn the repair side, but it also gives the company time to stop replacing departures. My screen work is exposed in 2031; robots around 2034 might later affect the repair crews. I cannot call either unit safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d shadow the repair dispatch manager one morning a month and ask whether they have a paid supervisor route. I’d keep using the approved AI tool to check simple warranty cases against our records. In 2031, if the service unit shrinks, I’d apply for repair coordination jobs and commute if the pay covers travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I can see a sequence. The first step is finding out what dispatch actually does, not buying a course because a headline frightened me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the commute worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It has to cover fares and leave more take-home pay than I have now. My partner’s bakery shifts start early, so I cannot assume we could move together. I would calculate it from an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could repair coordination also be automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the booking and route plans could be. I’m trying to learn the exceptions: a part delayed, a customer whose fridge is gone, a technician who cannot make the visit. I would test whether anyone still pays a person to settle those.

say: **Five years** lets staff test paid paths into appeals and repair coordination.
I’d ask the director to move people while those **openings** exist.
think: My **screen work** is exposed by 2031, with repair robots following around 2034.
A repair route may narrow too, so I need to test **paid exceptions**.
do: **Shadow** repair dispatch monthly starting this quarter.
**Check** simple warranty cases with the approved AI tool and company records.
**Apply** after 2031 for repair coordination only if travel costs leave higher take-home pay.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test a route before moving.
S3.quote: The first step is finding out what dispatch actually does, not buying a course because a headline frightened me.
fieldNote: He treats a **longer runway** as time to shadow dispatch before choosing a paid route, rather than buying speculative training.
The **commute** remains conditional on fares, take-home pay and his partner’s early shifts.

steps.text: Shadow the repair dispatch manager one morning each month
Check warranty cases using the approved AI tool and company records
Apply after 2031 for repair coordination if fares leave higher take-home pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives our company a decade to stop treating training as a last-minute apology. I’d want a published path from service work to repair oversight and a yearly review of which posts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our pay holds, my partner and I could clear the MBA debt and put several months of bills away. Thinking AI in 2036 could still remove my current reporting and queue planning; robots around 2039 would change repair work after that. I could be running a unit by then, but I would not build our finances on a title I do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’ll put any pay rise first toward the loan, then a rent buffer, and I’ll request one paid rotation in repair dispatch and take it if approved. I’ll review openings each year rather than move on a guess. In the first year after 2036, I’d take a repair oversight post only if the pay and work are still there; otherwise I’d seek a service role at another firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but I can breathe in this version. The time lets us make a household plan instead of an emergency call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we should see whether one pay rise can clear the loan faster, and keep bakery income for ordinary bills. I cannot order my partner’s hours around my career idea. We would check the numbers together on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the company publish first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The jobs it expects to keep, what each pays and who can train during work hours. A training catalogue without vacancies is a nice poster. I would ask for the pay bands in writing.

say: A **decade** should bring a published path into repair oversight and yearly job reviews.
I’d ask for **paid training** tied to actual vacancies.
think: We could clear the **MBA debt** and save several months of bills if wages hold.
My current desk duties remain **exposed** in 2036, before repair robots around 2039.
do: **Put** any 2026 pay rise toward the loan, then a rent buffer.
**Request** a paid repair dispatch rotation and take it if approved.
**Review** real openings yearly and apply after 2036 if service roles vanish.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to plan alongside his partner.
S4.quote: A training catalogue without vacancies is a nice poster.
fieldNote: He ties **training** to paid posts and written pay bands, reflecting his practical view of what firms owe workers.
The **household plan** relies on wage growth; he does not presume his partner’s bakery hours can absorb a career gamble.

steps.text: Put any pay rise toward MBA debt and then a rent buffer
Take a paid repair dispatch rotation if the company approves it
Review real service and repair openings once each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our service desk could shrink before we have rent money saved. I would need dates, severance in numbers, and paid training linked to a vacancy. My partner and I can plan around a hard answer; we cannot plan around a cheerful poster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the person whose claim the machine gets wrong. A customer cannot eat a fast response time. Someone has to fix the fridge and say who will pay.

headlineQuote: My partner and I can plan around a hard answer; we cannot plan around a cheerful poster.
portrait: **Omar, 27**, leads eleven people in a large appliance company’s returns and service unit after earning an MBA.
His **low pay**, MBA loan and partner’s variable bakery hours leave less than one month of expenses saved.
He sometimes uses **AI drafting**, tests its customer outcomes and asks for paid paths into repair coordination.
He is **uneasy** in AI Plateau, anxious under steady change and alarmed by AGI in 2028, when his desk work could vanish.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut service jobs before his household builds enough rent savings.
whatWouldHelp: Written **dates and severance**, plus paid training tied to an actual vacancy, would let the household plan.
